1.goal: To see what he produces BEFORE any explanation. Whatever comes out here is the baseline for the day.
1.interaction: T–S, two sentences from you, then straight on.
run: Tell him this is the lesson he asked for in July — he asked for conditionals in writing, in meeting 21.
Then go straight to the case on the next screen.
Teach nothing yet. Stage 1 is diagnostic, and an explanation here costs you the only unprompted sample of the lesson.
1.expected: Recognition that this is the lesson he asked for. Nothing to produce yet.
1.support: If he asks what the rule is, say it comes at stage 4, and that you want to hear him do it first.
1.challenge: Ask him to predict which of the two — the form or the speed — will be the difficulty today.
1.monitoring: Whether he reaches for the rule before trying. That reflex is the object of the whole lesson.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The sample starts on the next screen.
1.transition: Move on when he has tried once, right or wrong.

2.goal: One hypothetical sentence, produced with no support, on a case he has just read.
2.interaction: S reads alone for a minute, then one sentence out loud to you.
run: Give him one minute to read the summary.
Then ask the question below and let it come out however it comes out.
Do not correct. Note it and move — the correction belongs to stage 5, and correcting now turns the diagnostic into a lesson.
exact: In one sentence — what would have been different?
2.expected: One sentence about the delayed statement. The form may or may not appear; either way it is the measurement.
2.support: If nothing comes at all, ask what the eleven days changed. Do not offer the structure.
2.challenge: Ask for a second sentence about the same fact, from the other side's point of view.
2.monitoring: Whether the form appears on its own. The teacher record says he recognizes conditionals and completes exercises, and stalls on them in conversation. This is where that shows.
2.evidence: His sentence, word for word. It is the unprompted sample of the day and it comes back at stage 9.
2.transition: Move on when he has said one sentence.

3.goal: To hear the objection before having to answer it.
3.interaction: S listens, then T–S on the two questions.
run: Read the two questions WITH him before you play.
Play once.
Then ask which of Owen's three sentences is the hardest to answer.
3.expected: He grants the delay and refuses the conclusion. The hardest is the third — “even if you are right about the timing, it would not change what the witness says today” — because it concedes and gives nothing away.
3.support: If the third sentence reads as agreement, play it again and ask what Owen has actually given up by saying it.
3.challenge: Ask what he would say back to the third one, right now, before the lesson teaches it.
3.monitoring: Whether he reads the concession as a move rather than a retreat. That reading is what stage 5 then teaches him to produce.
3.evidence: How he names Owen's third move — it is the form he will have to produce under objection at stage 8.
3.transition: Move on when he has named the concession as a move.

4.goal: To separate three moves that arrive together in real speech: the fact, the hypothetical, and the concession.
4.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S on the order of the moves.
run: He classifies the six on his own, then Check — each wrong line shows what it was, and the explanation opens with it.
Then ask which of the three he does first in an oral submission.
Say out loud that he builds this argument in Portuguese with precision, by profession. The difficulty is not the reasoning; it is reaching the form in time.
exact: In an oral submission, which of the three do you do first?
“Had she been asked that night” — did it happen? (No.) Is it the same as “if she had been asked”? (Yes, and more formal.)
4.expected: A fact from the summary: the statement taken eleven days later, and she had already spoken to two other people · what would have been different: “if it had been taken that night…” and “had she been asked that night…” · a concession: “even if the delay explains some of it…” and “that is a fair point…”. The answer to the question is the fact — always.
4.support: If the inverted form reads as a different structure, put the two versions side by side and ask what changed besides the word order.
4.challenge: Ask him to say the same claim three times — fact first, hypothetical first, concession first — and which order Owen would find hardest.
4.monitoring: Whether he hesitates on the inverted form. Hesitation here predicts the stall at stage 8.
4.evidence: Whether the three moves are already separate for him, or arrive as one block.
4.transition: Move on when he recognizes the inverted form without hesitating.

5.goal: The concession that does NOT give the point away.
5.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S over the form and the reduction.
run: He marks the two that keep the point, then Check opens the explanation.
The point is the SECOND move — the turn. Without it the sentence stops at the concession and lands as surrender.
Form: “even if” + present or past subjunctive (“were”) for the present hypothetical; “even if” + past perfect for the past.
Pronunciation: “would not have been” reduces to “wouldn't-uv-bin” in real speech. Say it twice and ask for it back — the reduction is part of what makes the form reachable in time.
5.expected: The two that keep it: “Even if that were true, it would not change the timeline” and “That is fair — the difference is she had spoken to two people first”. The other two concede and stop.
5.support: If the turn keeps disappearing, ask what is still true after the concession. That question produces the second half of the sentence.
5.challenge: Ask for a concession with a turn about a case of his own, on the spot.
5.monitoring: Whether the second half arrives on its own or has to be asked for every time.
5.evidence: Whether he can produce a concession with a turn unsupported. It is the form stage 8 puts under pressure.
5.transition: Move on when he produces a concession with a turn, unsupported.

6.goal: To automate the form before pressure enters.
6.interaction: T gives the fact; S gives the hypothetical. Eight of them, fast.
run: You give the fact, he gives the hypothetical — one sentence. Eight of them, fast, without discussing the content.
Then eight concessions with a turn.
Pace is the whole point here. If he stops to think for more than three seconds, say the sentence yourself and move on.
This stage measures speed of access, not accuracy — accuracy was already measured in the pre-class.
exact: When the three seconds pass, say the whole sentence and move: “If it had been taken that night, we would not be arguing about it now.”
6.expected: Eight hypotheticals and eight concessions, at speed. Content does not matter here; latency does.
6.support: Drop to four-word prompts if the sentences get long. The shorter the input, the faster the access.
6.challenge: Alternate the two types without warning him which is coming.
6.monitoring: How long the pause is before each sentence, and whether it shortens across the eight.
6.evidence: How many come out without a long pause. It is the measure of access, and it goes in the record.
6.transition: Move on when four in a row come out without a long pause, or at seven minutes.

7.goal: The same form, now on his own material.
7.interaction: T–S. He talks; you ask one question at the end.
run: Ask for ONE decision in his own work that turned on something happening at the wrong moment — too late, too early, out of order. No names, no identifying detail.
Then: say what would have been different, and answer “what does that change now?” before you ask it.
Let him talk. This is the point in the lesson where his long turns work for him: the content is his, and the form has to appear inside it.
exact: The question he has to answer before you ask it: “And what does that change now?”
7.expected: A hypothetical about the past, followed by a consequence in the present.
7.support: If the consequence stays in the past, ask where the case is today. The present tense follows the question.
7.challenge: Ask for the same pair in two sentences instead of one, and then in one again.
7.monitoring: Whether the consequence lands in the PRESENT (“we would not be arguing about it now”) rather than staying in the past. That pairing is what the next stage is built on.
7.evidence: The case he chooses and the pair he produces. It is the material of the production stage.
7.transition: Move on when he has produced the pair: hypothetical, then consequence now.

8.goal: The product of the lesson — three hypothetical claims held against objection, with no written support.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Owen, and you disagree with each claim.
run: Disagree with EACH of the three.
On the third, bring in a new fact that weakens what he said, and let him adjust the claim.
If he repeats the sentence unchanged instead of reformulating it, let him. That is evidence, not an error to correct on the spot.
Object in one sentence, then stop talking. The turn is his.
exact: The new fact for the third claim: “She had already given a written note to the police on the night — it just was not signed.”
8.expected: Three claims, each restated after being contradicted, with the form surviving the second attempt.
8.support: If the third claim collapses entirely, ask what is still true after the new fact. Do not supply the sentence.
8.challenge: Object twice to the same claim and see whether the third version is shorter than the second.
8.monitoring: Not whether the form comes out, but whether it comes out AGAIN after being contradicted. The teacher record says he identifies and completes and stalls in conversation; this is where that is decided.
8.evidence: What happens to the form on the second attempt of each claim. It is the main evidence of the block.
8.transition: Move on when all three have been contested.

9.goal: To give back two points and ask for the same claim once more, now that he knows the objection that is coming.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the fields together, then one retask.
run: Fill the fields on screen with him — two points, no more.
Then the SAME claim, in one sentence, said so that the objection is already answered.
No new content here. Same task, one changed condition.
exact: The retask: “Same claim, one sentence, with Owen's objection already answered inside it.”
9.expected: One sentence carrying the fact, the hypothetical and the concession together.
9.support: If the three moves will not fit in one sentence, ask which of them Owen already accepts — that one can go.
9.challenge: Ask for the same sentence again with the inverted form.
9.monitoring: If the form came out in the first turn and not in the second, the difficulty is RECOVERY under real-time pressure, not understanding. If it came out in neither, the rule is not yet available to him.
9.evidence: Those two readings send block 2 in opposite directions, and this is the lesson that separates them — it is the first of the two open points in the profile. Record which one it is.
9.transition: Move on when the claim has been said once more, in one sentence.

10.goal: To name what the lesson worked on, and to leave the next one announced.
10.interaction: T–S over the list; the confidence row is his alone.
run: Read the list with him. The confidence row is his.
Homework, said out loud and never put on screen: the post-class has Julia Dhar on why conceding strengthens an argument — the exact move of stage 5 — and the BBC unit with the written form.
Announce lesson 12: it closes the block. He presents the position to someone from another jurisdiction who does not know what a jury court is, and absorbs ONE objection of substance.
10.expected: One phrase named as usable, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is named, ask which sentence from stage 6 he would have wanted in the last discussion he lost.
10.challenge: Ask when the next discussion like this one is, and which of the three moves he will use first.
10.monitoring: A confident mark on the form with a stall at stage 8 is the gap this lesson exists to measure. Note the two together.
10.evidence: This is the lesson that produces the main evidence for the lesson that closes the block. Fill in the post-lesson record carefully, especially what changed between the first turn and the retask.
